notes.heading: Types of organic formulas
points: Empirical formula gives the simplest atom ratio; molecular formula gives actual atom numbers. Glucose: C6H12O6 molecular, CH2O empirical.
Neither empirical nor molecular formula shows structure, so they cannot identify larger molecules.
Full (displayed) structural formula shows every atom and bond; condensed shows atoms in order with some or all bonds omitted.
Skeletal formula: carbons sit at line ends and corners, hydrogens on carbon are not drawn, functional-group atoms are drawn.
Double bond = two lines, triple bond = three lines. Stereochemical formulas use wedges and dashes for 3D shape.

notes.heading: Functional groups and classes
points: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms giving a compound its characteristic physical and chemical properties.
Compounds with the same functional group form a class and react similarly. R stands for any carbon-containing group.
Groups: halogeno (R-X), hydroxyl (-OH, alcohol), carbonyl (aldehyde RCHO, ketone RCOR'), carboxyl (-COOH), alkoxy (ether), amino, amido, ester, phenyl.
Saturated: only single C-C bonds, e.g. alkanes. Unsaturated: at least one C=C or C≡C, e.g. alkenes.

notes.heading: Homologous series and general formulas
points: A homologous series has members differing by one CH2 unit, with the same functional group and a shared general formula.
Alkanes CnH2n+2; alkenes CnH2n; alkynes CnH2n-2; halogenoalkanes CnH2n+1X.
Alcohols CnH2n+1OH; aldehydes and ketones CnH2nO; carboxylic acids CnH2nO2; amines CnH2n+3N; amides CnH2n+1NO.
Aldehyde carbonyl is at the chain end; ketone carbonyl is within the chain. Esters are RCO2R'; ethers are ROR'.
Amines: primary, secondary, tertiary by number of carbons bonded to nitrogen (1, 2, 3).

notes.heading: Physical trends in a series
points: Members share chemical properties because they have the same functional group.
Boiling and melting points rise with chain length because London (dispersion) forces strengthen as molar mass increases.
Boiling point trend is smooth and predictable; melting point trend is less regular and less reliable for prediction.
Density and viscosity also increase with chain length.
Fractional distillation of crude oil uses different boiling points: longer chains condense lower in the column, shorter ones higher.

notes.heading: IUPAC naming rules
points: Name = prefixes (substituents, alphabetical) + root from the longest chain containing the principal group + suffix. Root names: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex.
Number the chain so the principal group, then double bond, then substituents get the lowest locants. Locants are separated from letters by hyphens, from each other by commas.
Identical substituents take di, tri, tetra. Alkyl substituents end -yl, e.g. methyl. Example: 2,3-dimethylhexane.
Suffixes: -ene (C=C), -ol (alcohol), -al (aldehyde, carbon 1), -one (ketone), -oic acid (carboxylic acid), -amine. Halogens are prefixes fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo.
Locants are omitted when only one position is possible, e.g. bromoethane, propanone. Secondary and tertiary amines use N- for groups on nitrogen.

notes.heading: Structural isomers
points: Structural isomers share a molecular formula but differ in how atoms are connected.
Chain isomers differ in carbon chain, e.g. butane and methylpropane (C4H10).
Positional isomers differ in the position of the functional group, e.g. 1-, 2- and 3-bromopentane.
Functional group isomers have different groups, e.g. ethanol and methoxymethane, propanal and propanone, ethanoic acid and methyl methanoate.
Alcohol or halogenoalkane class: count carbons attached to the carbon bearing the group (1, 2, 3). Amines: count carbons on nitrogen.

notes.heading: Stereoisomers and chirality
points: Stereoisomers have the same connectivity and bond multiplicity but different spatial arrangement. Conformers interconvert by single-bond rotation; configurational isomers need bonds broken.
Cis-trans isomers need restricted rotation (C=C or ring) and two different groups on each unsaturated carbon. Propene has none.
A chiral carbon has four different groups. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images; the compound is optically active.
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions, (+) clockwise and (-) anticlockwise. A 50:50 racemic mixture does not rotate it.
Enantiomers behave identically in non-chiral environments but differently in chiral ones, such as biological molecules.
Stereochemical drawings: plain line in the paper plane, wedge towards viewer, dash away; draw the mirror image for the other enantiomer.

notes.heading: Mass spectrometry
points: MS breaks molecules into fragments, some ions; the peaks form the fragmentation pattern.
The peak with the highest m/z is the molecular ion, giving the relative molecular mass.
Fragment peaks match groups lost or kept, e.g. m/z 15 CH3, 29 CHO or C2H5, 31 CH2OH, 45 COOH.
Chlorine has two isotopes (35 and 37), so chlorine compounds show extra peaks, giving molecular ion peaks at several m/z values.

notes.heading: Infrared spectroscopy
points: Bonds absorb IR radiation and vibrate (stretching or bending); absorptions in cm-1 identify bond types and so functional groups.
Wavenumber = 1/wavelength. Stronger bonds and lighter atoms vibrate at higher frequency.
A vibration must change the dipole moment to be IR active; H2, O2 and Cl2 are inactive.
Example: carbonyl C=O absorbs strongly near 1700-1750 cm-1; carboxylic acid O-H gives a very broad peak around 2500-3000 cm-1.
H2O and CO2 absorb IR in stretching and bending modes. IR alone shows groups, not the full structure.

notes.heading: Proton NMR spectra
points: 1H NMR shows the number of different hydrogen environments: one signal per environment, symmetric equivalent hydrogens share a signal.
Chemical shift δ in ppm is measured relative to TMS at 0 ppm.
Integration trace or peak area is proportional to the number of hydrogens in each environment, giving a ratio.
Example: ethanoic acid gives two signals in 1:3 ratio; propanone gives a single signal.
Nuclei in a strong magnetic field have two spin energy levels; radio waves of matching energy cause resonance.

notes.heading: Splitting of NMR signals
points: In high resolution spectra, signals split into clusters by spin-spin coupling with hydrogens on neighbouring atoms.
N + 1 rule: N neighbouring hydrogens give N + 1 peaks. Equivalent hydrogens do not split each other.
Patterns: singlet 1, doublet 1:1, triplet 1:2:1, quartet 1:3:3:1 (Pascal's triangle).
Example: in butanone, CH3 next to CH2 is a triplet, CH2 is a quartet and the CH3CO is a singlet.

notes.heading: Combining analytical data
points: Structure deduction combines several sources: combustion analysis (empirical formula), MS, IR, 1H NMR, data booklet and reactions.
Empirical formula: divide each percentage by relative atomic mass, then divide by the smallest value.
Molecular ion m/z gives the relative molecular mass, compared with the empirical formula mass to find the molecular formula.
IR gives groups present, MS gives fragments, NMR gives hydrogen environments and neighbours; together they fix the structure.

definitions.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with the molecular formula, which gives actual numbers of atoms.

definitions.definition: The actual number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a compound.
definitions.trap: Giving the simplest ratio instead of the actual numbers.

definitions.definition: A representation showing how the atoms in a molecule are arranged and bonded, unlike a molecular formula.
definitions.trap: Treating a molecular formula as a structural formula.

definitions.definition: A structural formula where lines represent bonds, carbon is at each vertex and line end, hydrogens on carbon are omitted and functional-group atoms are shown.
definitions.trap: Forgetting that atoms in the functional group, such as O, must still be drawn.

definitions.definition: An atom or group of atoms in a molecule that gives the compound its characteristic physical and chemical properties.
definitions.trap: Saying it is the whole molecule rather than a specific part.

definitions.definition: A hydrocarbon in which all carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds.
definitions.trap: Defining it by solutions (no more solute dissolves), as examiners note.

definitions.definition: A compound containing at least one carbon-carbon double or triple bond.
definitions.trap: Stating only double bonds and omitting triple bonds.

definitions.definition: A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by a CH2 unit.
definitions.trap: Saying members have identical physical properties; only chemical properties are similar.

definitions.definition: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms.
definitions.trap: Writing 'similar' formula instead of 'same' molecular formula, as weaker candidates did.

definitions.definition: Compounds with the same connectivity and bond multiplicity but different spatial arrangement of atoms.
definitions.trap: Giving the definition of structural isomers instead.

definitions.definition: A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups of atoms.
definitions.trap: Counting a carbon with two identical groups, such as two methyls, as chiral.

definitions.definition: A pair of stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
definitions.trap: Omitting non-superimposable; any mirror image of a symmetric molecule is superimposable.

definitions.definition: A 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers, which does not rotate plane-polarized light.
The ability of a chiral compound to rotate the plane of plane-polarized light.
definitions.trap: Thinking both enantiomers rotate it in the same direction.

definitions.definition: The ion formed when a molecule loses one electron in mass spectrometry, giving the peak of highest m/z and the relative molecular mass.
definitions.trap: Assuming the tallest peak is the molecular ion rather than the highest m/z.

definitions.definition: The reciprocal of wavelength, used in IR spectra and measured in cm-1.
definitions.trap: Mixing it up with frequency or wavelength.

definitions.definition: The position of an NMR signal, in ppm, relative to the tetramethylsilane (TMS) standard set at 0.
definitions.trap: Forgetting that TMS is the reference.

definitions.definition: A set of internationally agreed rules from the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry for systematically naming organic and inorganic compounds.
definitions.trap: Using common names, such as formic acid, where a systematic name is required.
